source: Slade (1991) Case-Based Reasoning: A Research Paradigm (AI Magazine 12:1)
finding: Review of the founding Schank/Kolodner/Hammond line. CBR rests on a memory model (cases indexed in episodic memory) and a process model (retrieve, modify, test, store). It grew out of Schank's scripts, then Memory Organization Packets (MOPs), and the idea that reminding and learning are one memory process.
numbers: No experiment. Names the 1979-1989 systems: CYRUS (1980), IPP, MEDIATOR (1985), JUDGE (1986), CHEF (1984-89), HYPO (1987).
quote: Case-based reasoning is a general paradigm for reasoning from experience.
limits: A narrative review by one author; it describes systems, it does not test them.
agent_relevance: Gives the original vocabulary for our S9 record: case = problem + solution + outcome, with an index chosen for later reminding.

source: Slade (1991) Case-Based Reasoning: A Research Paradigm - the six-step cycle (after Riesbeck and Bain 1987)
finding: The original CBR loop has six steps: assign indexes, retrieve, modify, test, assign and store (if it worked), explain-repair-test (if it failed). Failure is the learning trigger: explaining a failure adds the predictive feature to the indexing rules so the problem is anticipated next time.
numbers: 6 steps; 4 knowledge structures (indexing rules, modification rules, repair rules, case memory).
quote: The predictive features of the problem are incorporated into the indexing rules to anticipate this problem in the future.
limits: Indexing, modification and repair rules are hand-built in the early systems. Slade says the theory expects them to be learned from cases recursively, but early systems did not do this.
agent_relevance: Maps onto our states: the 'test' step is a code check (G2, G3). The step 'explain failure then add an index' is a design we do not yet have: a failure should change how a case is indexed, not only be stored.

source: Slade (1991) on CHEF (Hammond 1984, 1986, 1989)
finding: CHEF plans recipes by retrieving the most similar old recipe, modifying it, simulating it with rules on the physical effects of cooking, explaining any goal failure, repairing, and storing the repair so the mistake is not repeated. Example: strawberry souffle adapted from vanilla fails to rise because of excess liquid; the repair adds whipped egg whites; the lesson later helps a raspberry souffle.
numbers: One worked example; no success rates in the review.
quote: CHEF tries not to make the same mistake twice.
limits: Domain-specific repair strategies (ingredient substitution). Retrieval picks the old plan that matches the most new goals, then trial and error. No held-out evaluation in the review.
agent_relevance: Closest ancestor of 'retrieve a subgoal plan, run it, repair it from real failing output, store the repair'. Matches G2 (revise from real output) and G3 (test the revision on something not fitted).

source: Slade (1991) on MEDIATOR, JUDGE, CYRUS (Simpson 1985; Bain 1986; Kolodner 1980)
finding: MEDIATOR picks a precedent dispute (the Korean territory split); the proposal fails for the Sinai case because the goals differ, and the failure explanation leads to a different precedent. JUDGE retrieves past sentences. CYRUS organised an episodic memory of events about one official and answered questions by indexed retrieval.
numbers: No accuracy numbers in the review; qualitative demonstrations.
limits: Early CBR systems were demonstrations in narrow domains; the review gives no baseline comparison.
agent_relevance: A retrieved case can be wrong in its goals even if similar on the surface: reject on a goal mismatch, then re-retrieve. This is the 'reject a retrieved case' branch of SUBFIELDS question (b).

source: Slade (1991) on the persistent indexing problem (Schank, Collins, Hunter 1986)
finding: Slade names 'determining the significant input features' as a persistent problem for indexing. Remindings in people (the steak and the haircut) cross domains because they share an abstract expectation failure, not surface features.
numbers: Qualitative anecdotes gathered by Schank from colleagues and students; no sample size.
quote: Determining the significant input features is a persistent problem.
limits: Anecdotal; informal collection of remindings, not a controlled study.
agent_relevance: The index is the weak point. A subgoal library keyed only on embeddings of the problem text will find surface twins, not structural twins.

source: Kolodner (1991) Improving Human Decision Making through Case-Based Decision Aiding (AI Magazine 12:2)
finding: People use cases naturally and well, especially under uncertainty and in early learning, but retrieve poorly. Experts (car mechanics, physicians, architects, caterers) recall, merge and adapt old cases. Weaknesses: people reuse cases without validating them, are biased by them, and often are not reminded of the best case.
numbers: Qualitative report of lab observations (Lancaster and Kolodner 1988; Redmond 1989); no numbers.
quote: People tend to use surface features for retrieval when they are unfamiliar with a task or domain.
limits: Review and position paper; the human studies are cited, not re-run. Psychology claims are second-hand.
agent_relevance: The human failure list is also the LLM failure list: reuse without validation (G2/G3 fix this) and retrieval that misses the right case. Supports a code-run check on every adapted case.

source: Kolodner (1991) citing Klein and Calderwood (1988), Klein, Whitaker and King (1988)
finding: Naturalistic decision makers used analogs to understand dynamics, generate options and predict outcomes; analogs mattered more than abstract rules or deliberation among alternatives. Klein and Whitaker reported the case-based method was much more reliable than unstructured prediction when many things were unknown.
numbers: No numbers in Kolodner's summary.
limits: Second-hand. Naturalistic observation with no control condition described. Same material as the recognition-primed decision subfield (covered in parallel).
agent_relevance: Cases help most when the problem has many unknowns. For a well-specified problem a code check beats a case.

source: Kolodner (1991) on the pragmatics of indexing
finding: CBR research does not argue about surface versus abstract features. It says the right index depends on which reasoning task the case serves and which description of the old case explains its outcome. A machine can retrieve cases a novice could not, and can show failed cases with explanations so users do not discount them.
numbers: None.
quote: Sometimes surface features are the right ones to index on, sometimes abstract features.
limits: A design argument, not an experiment.
agent_relevance: Use task-dependent indexes: index each subgoal case by goal, preconditions and the failure it avoided, and show stored failures as visible warnings.

source: Nguyen, Czerwinski, Lee (1993) COMPAQ QuickSource (IAAI-93), reporting Compaq SMART
finding: Early fielded CBR. SMART used case-based reasoning to help Compaq support staff; QuickSource (QuickSolve cases) put it in the customer's hands. Compaq reported about 20 percent fewer calls for the printer line than a comparison product and estimated 10 to 20 million dollars per year saved.
numbers: About 500 cases audited; 20 percent fewer calls; one-week call sample; error margin about 5 percent; saving 10 to 20 million dollars a year (extrapolated).
limits: Exact figures withheld as confidential. The comparison is between two product lines (printer vs server) adjusted by expert judgement of complexity. Vendor report, not a controlled trial.
agent_relevance: A small curated case base pays off when case structure is uniform and uses focusing questions. Software and network cases were kept shallow.

source: Gick and Holyoak (1980, 1983) as reported by Loewenstein, Thompson, Gentner (1999)
finding: Duncker radiation problem: about 10 percent solve it alone. After reading the analogous fortress story and being told to use it, solution rose to about 85 percent. People kept the story but did not retrieve it on their own.
numbers: About 10 percent baseline; about 85 percent with a hint to use the analog (as quoted). Original sample sizes not read.
limits: Second-hand figures as stated in the 1999 paper; the 1980/83 papers were not opened. Same material belongs to the Transfer subfield.
agent_relevance: The retrieval step, not the reuse step, is where people fail. Put retrieval in code and add an explicit instruction to apply the retrieved case.

source: Gentner, Rattermann, Forbus (1993) as reported by Loewenstein, Thompson, Gentner (1999)
finding: Retrieval of stories from memory is driven by surface similarity. Probe stories matching on surface features cued recall 55 percent of the time; purely relational matches only 12 percent. Yet relational matches alone were rated useful for inference.
numbers: 55 percent versus 12 percent recall (as quoted).
limits: Second-hand; original not opened. The MAC/FAC model of this finding is a parallel subfield (Analogical retrieval).
agent_relevance: A similarity-ranked case library has the same split: easy to retrieve (surface) is not what is useful (structure). Add a structural re-rank in code after the embedding fetch.

source: Loewenstein, Thompson, Gentner (1999) Experiment 1A, baseline
finding: Without analogy training, undergraduates given two negotiation case studies almost always wrote compromises on the test case. Many were reminded of an earlier case but did not use its strategy.
numbers: N=16 undergraduates. 15 of 16 (94 percent) wrote at least one compromise; 3 of 16 (19 percent) used the tradeoff principle; 10 of 16 (63 percent) said they were reminded of a prior case.
limits: Small N, one university population, negotiation domain.
agent_relevance: Being reminded does not mean the case was applied. The agent needs a forced reuse step (adapt and run), not only a retrieval step.

source: Loewenstein, Thompson, Gentner (1999) Experiment 1B, maximal analogy training
finding: Intensive analogy training (comparing two cases of one principle) raised use of that same principle on a new negotiation. The gain was specific to the trained principle, which rules out general facilitation.
numbers: N=32 (16 per condition). Tradeoff training: 38 percent used tradeoffs (vs 19 percent baseline); contingency-contract training: 69 percent used contingency contracts (vs 6 percent and 0 percent in comparison cells). Overall 50 percent transferred the taught solution versus 19 percent baseline.
limits: N=32; effect on one principle is stronger than on the other. Negotiation only.
agent_relevance: Comparing two stored cases to extract the shared principle beats storing a single case. Supports a library entry that holds a merged schema from at least two cases.

source: Loewenstein, Thompson, Gentner (1999) Experiment 2, minimal comparison
finding: Even a light prompt to compare two cases, versus reading them one after another, increased transfer of the contingency contract in new negotiations (dyads). Schema quality written by compare dyads was higher. Adding an abstract label did not help.
numbers: Contingency contract used by 13 of 27 compare dyads (48 percent) versus 5 of 31 no-compare dyads (16 percent); chi-square p < .005 reported; labelling added nothing (30 percent label vs 32 percent no-label).
limits: Dyads, one domain, one principle. Tradeoffs were not retested in Experiment 2.
agent_relevance: Compare cases in pairs when they are added and write the shared structure into the record. An abstract label alone does not do it.

source: Wiratunga et al. (2024) CBR-RAG: Case-Based Reasoning for Retrieval Augmented Generation in LLMs for Legal QA
finding: Uses the CBR retrieval step and case representation (question, support, answer, entities) inside a RAG pipeline. Compares BERT, LegalBERT and AnglEBERT embeddings and inter, intra and hybrid similarity. Hybrid AnglEBERT with k=3 gives the best answer similarity.
numbers: Case base 2,084 cases (2,124 minus 40). Test set 32 questions. Cosine score against reference: No-RAG 0.8967; Hybrid AnglEBERT k=3 0.9141 (about 1.94 percent gain); significant over No-RAG at 95 percent (one-tailed t-test). Hybrid weights [0.25, 0.40, 0.35].
limits: Tiny test set (32 questions written by Mistral-7B from case pairs). The metric is embedding cosine to a reference, not human or factual grading. Gain is small. The No-RAG baseline is already high because of parametric memory.
agent_relevance: Weak evidence that case structure helps; the lesson is to index on several fields of a case (question, support, entities) and weight them.

source: Zhao et al. (2024) ExpeL: LLM Agents Are Experiential Learners (AAAI 2024)
finding: Agent gathers success and failure trajectories on training tasks, extracts natural-language insights (ADD, UPVOTE, DOWNVOTE, EDIT), and retrieves similar successful trajectories as in-context examples at test time. Both parts matter.
numbers: HotpotQA success: ReAct 28.0 vs ExpeL 39.0. ALFWorld: ReAct 40.0 vs ExpeL 59.0; ExpeL retrieve-only 54.5 at first attempt. WebShop: insights-only 37 percent vs retrieve-only 38 percent. Tasks: 134 ALFWorld, 100 HotpotQA, 100 WebShop, four-fold.
limits: gpt-3.5 / gpt-4 era. Environments are deterministic with repeated task templates, which helps retrieval.
agent_relevance: A working retrieve-plus-abstract memory for LLM agents with measured gains. Retrieval of a similar trajectory is strong where tasks repeat.

source: Zhao et al. (2024) ExpeL ablations: how to retrieve
finding: Ranking retrieved cases by task similarity beat both random sampling and reasoning-step similarity. Hand-written insights helped less than LLM insights, and adding reflections to insight extraction hurt.
numbers: ALFWorld success: ReAct 40.0; reasoning-similarity retrieval 48.5; random 42.5; task-similarity (ExpeL) 59.0. HotpotQA: ReAct 28.0; hand-crafted insights 32.0; insights with reflections 29.0; gpt-3.5 insights 32.0; ExpeL (gpt-4 insights) 39.0.
limits: Retrieval-key choice tested only on ALFWorld; insight ablation only on HotpotQA.
agent_relevance: Random cases are close to useless (42.5 vs 40.0). The index matters more than having a store. Use task-level keys rather than step-level ones.

source: Zhao et al. (2024) ExpeL transfer and Reflexion pairing
finding: Insights from HotpotQA transferred to FEVER when re-grounded with a few target demonstrations. Combining ExpeL with Reflexion retries raised ALFWorld success further.
numbers: FEVER success: Act 58, ReAct 63, ExpeL transfer without task demos 65, ExpeL transfer 70. ALFWorld R0 to R3: ReAct+Reflexion 40.3 to 54.4; ExpeL retrieve-only 54.5 to 60.4; ExpeL+Reflexion 59.0 to 64.2.
limits: FEVER shares the tool interface with HotpotQA, so transfer is easy by design.
agent_relevance: Cases abstracted to insights moved across tasks only with a re-grounding step. Adapt a retrieved case to the new task before use.

source: Wang, Mao, Fried, Neubig (2024) Agent Workflow Memory
finding: Induces reusable workflows (a description plus steps) from past successful runs, offline or online, and gives them to the agent. Online induction (no training data) generalises better than offline as the train-test gap widens.
numbers: WebArena total success: BrowserGym baseline 23.5 vs AWM 35.5 (about 51 percent relative). Mind2Web claimed 24.6 percent relative gain. Mind2Web step success cross-domain: MindAct 18.6, AWM offline 32.6, AWM online 35.5. Task-level SR is very low there: 1.0 (MindAct), 0.7 (offline), 1.7 (online).
limits: Task-level success on Mind2Web stays under 5 percent in all arms; relative gains sit on small bases. Online workflows can be wrong when the model's own trajectories were wrong.
agent_relevance: A workflow is a subgoal case with a description key: the closest published match to our subgoal library by similarity.

source: Zheng et al. (2024) Synapse: Trajectory-as-Exemplar Prompting with Memory for Computer Control (ICLR 2024)
finding: Stores abstracted exemplar trajectories in a vector database keyed on task metadata. Retrieval gives the right exemplar nearly always on MiniWoB++, and the agent is reported as the first in-context method at human level.
numbers: MiniWoB++ mean success 99.2 percent; solves 64 tasks; exemplar mismatch caused only a 2 percent failure rate on click-tab-2-hard. Exemplar memory helps most on long-horizon tasks with repeated actions.
limits: MiniWoB++ has a small set of fixed templates, so retrieval is easy. Mind2Web results are smaller.
agent_relevance: Retrieval is nearly solved when the library is small and templated; the hard case is when it is not.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Voyager: skill library with embedding retrieval
finding: Each verified skill (code) is stored under an embedding of its generated description; for a new task the top-5 skills go in the prompt. Without the skill library progress plateaus in later stages. The library also helps AutoGPT when plugged in.
numbers: 63 unique items in 160 prompting iterations, 3.3 times the best baseline. Skill retrieval over 309 samples: top-1 80.2 percent (SD 3.0), top-5 96.5 percent. Random curriculum cuts discovered items by 93 percent.
limits: Minecraft only. Skills are code that can be run and verified, which is not true of most reasoning cases. Stored only after self-verification.
agent_relevance: A verified, executable skill library works. Matches G3 and a rule to store only verified entries.

source: Xiong et al. (2025) How Memory Management Impacts LLM Agents: experience-following
finding: Agents copy the output of the most similar retrieved case (experience-following). Errors propagate: wrong stored cases are repeated and re-stored. Adding every execution to memory hurts; adding only strictly verified ones helps.
numbers: Four agents, fixed memory vs add-all vs strict addition: RegAgent success 67.53 / 55.48 / 70.95; EHRAgent accuracy 16.75 / 13.05 / 38.50; AgentDriver success 40.11 / 32.32 / 51.00; CIC-IoT accuracy 71.50 / 59.90 / 85.40. Add-all memory grew to 4,100 / 2,411 / 2,125 / 1,050 records against fixed 100 / 100 / 180 / 50.
limits: The strict evaluator is a human oracle or exact match; coarse LLM evaluators gave weaker or negative effects. Four agents, not all reasoning tasks.
agent_relevance: Supports a gate on Retain. Store only cases that pass a held-out, code-run check (G3); add-all is worse than a frozen small library on all four agents.

source: Xiong et al. (2025) deletion and misaligned experience replay
finding: Some stored cases that looked correct are poor demonstrations later (misaligned experience replay). Deleting cases by downstream utility (history-based deletion) beats periodic deletion when the utility judge is reliable, and shrinks memory; with a noisy judge it can hurt.
numbers: A record is removed if retrieved at least 3 or 5 times with poor average downstream score (thresholds set per agent). With the strict judge, history-based deletion improved AgentDriver and near task 1000 surpassed its error-free memory variant.
limits: Needs enough retrievals per record to estimate utility. Results vary with the evaluator, task shift and memory cap. Case-base maintenance has its own parallel subfield.
agent_relevance: Maintain the library by measured reuse outcome, not age. Keep an outcome counter per case.

source: Gan, Dao, Zettsu (2025) CBR-LLM for safety-critical driving decisions
finding: Retrieves similar past near-miss driving cases as few-shot examples. Similarity retrieval beat random selection for every model tested. With random examples, one irrelevant example often lowered accuracy below zero-shot.
numbers: 1,000 dashcam events. Llama3.3-70B micro-accuracy 0.937 risk-unaware and 0.941 risk-aware. Accuracy rose steadily with 1 to 5 similar cases; 1-shot random often fell below zero-shot. DeepSeek-R1 14B got worse with more examples whatever the selection.
limits: Accuracy near ceiling for the best model, so gains are small. Few maneuver classes. Model-specific exception.
agent_relevance: A wrong case can be worse than none, and reasoning models may be hurt by examples. Include a no-case path (a retrieval threshold) and test per model.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Memento: Fine-tuning LLM Agents without Fine-tuning LLMs (case bank, Q-learned retrieval)
finding: Formalises CBR as a memory-augmented MDP: case = (state, action, reward); a policy retrieves a case, then an LLM acts. Compares non-parametric similarity retrieval (TopK on embeddings) with a parametric learned Q-function retrieval. The bank writes both successes and failures.
numbers: GAIA validation 87.88 percent Pass@3, test 79.40 percent; DeepResearcher 66.6 F1 and 80.4 PM; HLE 24.4 PM; SimpleQA 95.0 PM. DeepResearcher learning curve, iterations 1 to 5: no CBR 78.65 to 84.47; non-parametric CBR 79.84 to 84.85; parametric CBR 80.46 to 85.44.
limits: Gain of CBR over the no-CBR planner is modest and shrinks with iterations (at iteration 5: +0.4 and +1.0 points). The case bank saturates; training set about 3k items.
agent_relevance: A learned retrieval policy helps a little over plain similarity; much of the gain comes from the planner-executor design, not from CBR.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Memento ablations: number of cases K and component analysis
finding: A few retrieved cases are best; more add noise. CBR adds a consistent gain on top of planning; planning adds more than CBR; live tool access alone can hurt on contaminated QA sets.
numbers: DeepResearcher average F1/PM by K: K=0 59.9/72.2; K=2 63.6/77.9; K=4 64.5/78.5 (best); K=8 64.1/78.2; K=16 63.9/78.1; K=32 63.9/78.1 (columns as read from the table). CBR gain: HLE +4.5 F1 / +7.0 PM; SimpleQA +3.7 / +5.3; DeepResearcher +6.7 / +8.2. Planning gain: HLE +11.0/+1.6; SimpleQA +32.5/+4.9; DeepResearcher +29.1/+11.5. Out-of-distribution gain from cases 4.7 to 9.6 points.
quote: CBR benefits from a small, high-quality memory, unlike few-shot prompting.
limits: gpt-4.1 planner with o4-mini executor. Authors flag data contamination on DeepResearcher. No confidence intervals. Column-to-K mapping of Table 3 inferred from the text (K=4 best).
agent_relevance: Library size per query should be small (about 4). Case retrieval does not benefit from many shots the way plain few-shot prompting does.

source: Ouyang et al. (2025) ReasoningBank: strategy memory from success and failure
finding: Stores distilled reasoning strategies (not raw trajectories) from self-judged successes and failures and adds memory-aware test-time scaling. Beats raw-trajectory memory and success-only workflow memory (Synapse, AWM) on WebArena, Mind2Web and SWE-Bench-Verified.
numbers: WebArena overall success +8.3, +7.2, +4.6 points over no memory across three backbones; up to 20 percent relative and up to 16 percent fewer steps. On the cross-website Multi subset AWM gave no gain and even degraded while ReasoningBank gained +4.6 over the strongest baseline. MaTTS parallel k=5: 55.1 vs 52.4 vanilla TTS.
limits: Success labels are self-judged without ground truth, so judge error is not isolated. Authors are at Google.
agent_relevance: Supports storing failures as strategy items and keeping memory abstract so it travels across sites. Also shows a workflow memory can fail on cross-domain tasks.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large Language Models as Analogical Reasoners (ICLR 2024)
finding: Instead of retrieving cases from a store, the model is asked to recall three relevant past problems itself, then solve. Works for strong models; fails for weak ones. Self-generated knowledge plus exemplars helps coding.
numbers: GSM8K: GPT-3.5-turbo 0-shot 75.0, 0-shot CoT 75.8, 5-shot CoT 76.7, self-generated exemplars 77.8; text-davinci-003 5-shot 54.0 vs 61.0; PaLM2 80.7 vs 81.7. MATH: GPT-3.5 34.9 vs 37.3; PaLM2 34.3 vs 34.8. Codeforces Acc@1: 0-shot 8, 3-shot 11, self-generated exemplars 13, plus knowledge 15 percent.
limits: Gains over few-shot CoT are small on GSM8K (1.0 to 1.1 points on two models). With smaller models retrieved labelled exemplars beat self-generation; self-generation fails when the model has not learned related problems.
agent_relevance: Cases generated from the model's own memory are not a replacement for a verified library; the gain vanishes with weaker models and the cases are unchecked.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Case-Based or Rule-Based: How Do Transformers Do the Math? (ICML 2024)
finding: Uses 'case-based' to mean interpolation from nearby training examples. In Leave-Square-Out tests, models fine-tuned on addition score 100 percent on random splits but fail on held-out squares, which looks like reasoning from nearby cases and not from the rule. A Rule-Following Fine-Tune (RFFT) fixes it.
numbers: Left-out square of 441 samples out of about 10,000 (side 20). RFFT: fine-tuned on 1 to 5 digit addition, generalises to 12 digits with over 95 percent accuracy, over 40 points above scratchpad, with 100 training samples in one setup.
limits: Not the Schank/Kolodner CBR. It describes interpolation inside the weights. Fine-tuned small models and GPT-3.5, not scaffold agents.
agent_relevance: A caution: model-internal case-like behaviour is a weakness for rule-governed problems. For rule-based subgoals give the rule and a code step, not a similar example.

source: Tang et al. (2025) Agent KB: cross-domain experience sharing
finding: Hybrid retrieval of workflows at planning time and targeted diagnostic fixes at feedback time, with a disagreement gate meant to make retrieved knowledge enhance rather than disrupt the agent's reasoning. Auto-generated experiences match manual curation.
numbers: smolagents GAIA pass@3 55.2 to 73.9 (+18.7 points); OpenHands SWE-bench pass@1 24.3 to 28.3 (+4.0).
limits: Only abstract and introduction read closely. Large multi-part framework; not isolated against plain similarity retrieval.
agent_relevance: A code-side gate on whether to apply a retrieved case is in line with G1 and G5.

source: Zeng et al. (2024) On the Structural Memory of LLM Agents
finding: Compares memory structure (chunks, triples, atomic facts, summaries, mixed) and retrieval method (single-step, rerank, iterative). Different structures suit different tasks; mixed memory is more robust to noise; iterative retrieval is best.
numbers: Four tasks, six datasets. Exact scores were not extracted.
limits: Abstract and introduction read; tables not examined.
agent_relevance: Retrieval can be iterated (retrieve, refine the query, retrieve again), a CBR-style loop for the library.

source: Aamodt and Plaza (1994) Case-Based Reasoning: Foundational Issues, Methodological Variations and System Approaches (AI Communications 7:1)
finding: Standard formalisation: the four-R cycle Retrieve, Reuse, Revise, Retain. Could not be opened this session (every fetched copy returned an error page), so this line gives only the well-known cycle and relies on Slade 1991 for content actually read.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Not opened; do not cite figures from this line.
agent_relevance: Source of the 'retrieve, reuse, revise, retain' wording in SUBFIELDS; the older six-step form in Slade 1991 is the same loop.
